summary: A paper from IBM researchers on describing data so it can be shared across a network. They sort differences in how data is represented into three levels, starting with the very local, like character sets and number formats, and argue a data description language could help bridge them.

plainLanguage.summary: Different computers write down the same information in different ways. This paper suggests a common way to describe data so one computer can understand another's.

questions: data description language for shared data
subtitle: A notation for describing data structures across different computers

tldr.problem: When computers with different internal representations want to share data, the receiver does not know how to interpret bytes, character sets, or data structures. There is no standard way to describe what the data means.
tldr.mechanism: IBM researchers propose a descriptive language that annotates data with metadata about its structure, type, and representation. A data descriptor tells the receiver how the sender's data is organized so it can be transformed into the receiver's format.
tldr.outcome: The language is formal and detailed but remains theoretical. It influenced later work on network data standards and serialization formats.

today: RFC 242 is an informational paper and has not been obsoleted. It represents early research into network data formats. Later standards such as XDR (External Data Representation) and ASN.1 built on similar ideas and saw widespread adoption.

sections.title: The Data Sharing Problem
sections.content:
Early computer networks revealed that data sharing is hard when computers differ in fundamental ways. They use different character sets (ASCII versus EBCDIC), different number formats (ones-complement versus twos-complement), different word sizes (32-bit, 60-bit, 6-bit bytes), and different ways to organize collections of data.

The RFC classifies these differences into three levels: very local representation (bits and bytes), collection-level differences (ordering and size), and structural complexity (files with indexes, pointers, and cross-references).
sections.plainLanguage: Computer A writes a number one way, Computer B writes it another way. When they share data, the numbers look like garbage unless someone explains the difference.

sections.title: The Data Description Language
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a formal notation for describing data. Every data element has a type code such as F for floating-point, I for fixed-point, C for character, or B for bit. Nested structures are written in parentheses, like ((C,C),(F,F,I)) to describe a structure with two branches.

Data elements can be annotated with properties: a name to label parts, a lock specification for concurrency control, authorization codes for access control, and modifiers for repetition or conditions. The notation is precise but complex.

A descriptor can refer to previously defined structures and can select parts of a data set using path notation (like file system paths with dot notation).
sections.plainLanguage: The language lets you write a recipe for data: the types of values, how they are grouped, what to call each part, and what rules apply to it.

sections.title: Using the Descriptive Language
sections.content:
A network data management system would accept two descriptions: one saying how data is currently represented, and one saying how the copy should look. The system would use the descriptions to transform the data from one format to another automatically.

This approach differs from systems that specify the transformation algorithm directly. Instead, describing both the source and target formats lets the system figure out what conversions are needed.

The paper presents the notation and examples, including how to express arrays, conditional elements, and repeated structures. The intent is to provide a complete formal framework for data transformation in a network context.
sections.plainLanguage: You describe the data you have and the data you want, and the system figures out how to convert between them.

references.text: Cited in the RFC as an alternative approach for specifying data transformations.
